notes.meaning: Jesus repeats that he is the living bread who nourishes our souls. While regular food only feeds our physical bodies for a little while, Jesus provides eternal life to everyone who trusts in him.

The ancient Israelites were fed by bread from the sky during their forty years in the desert, yet every one of them eventually died. That miracle kept their bodies alive for a short time, but it could never save them from spiritual or eternal death.
Jesus presents himself as the true bread that came down from the highest heaven. Anyone who receives him will never die spiritually or face eternal death.
Jesus explains that he is alive and able to give lasting life to all who take him in by faith. He gives this life by offering his own body as a sacrifice on the cross for the sins of the whole world.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics understand Jesus' promise of bread as pointing to the Eucharist, fulfilled when he gave his body and blood at the Last Supper.

notes.meaning: The people in the crowd began arguing fiercely with one another about what Jesus meant. They thought he was talking about physical cannibalism, which was completely forbidden, because they could not understand his spiritual meaning.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics hold that the listeners understood Jesus correctly to mean eating his real flesh, and that Jesus did not correct their literal understanding.

notes.meaning: Jesus stresses that no one can have spiritual life without receiving him completely. Mentioning flesh and blood separately pointed to his sacrificial death on the cross, which believers must receive into their hearts by faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics teach that Jesus spoke literally and that believers must receive his actual flesh and blood in the Eucharist, where they consume the living, glorified Christ rather than dead flesh.

notes.meaning: Anyone who constantly trusts in Jesus and receives the benefits of his death has real spiritual life right now. Jesus also promises that he will raise them to life on the final day.

differ.view: The official Lutheran Confessions teach that John 6 describes "spiritual eating," which means believing in Christ through the gospel with the heart. Lutherans distinguish this from the Lord's Supper, teaching that this passage is about faith itself rather than receiving the physical bread and wine at the altar.
differ.disputed: eating his flesh: the Lord's Supper

differ.view: The Orthodox Presbyterian Church teaches that John 6 does not refer to the communion table, but entirely to Christ's sacrifice on the cross received by faith. While the Lord's Supper uses bread and wine as visible signs to point to that same cross, "eating" in John 6 simply means trusting in Jesus.
differ.disputed: eating his flesh: the Lord's Supper

differ.view: Baptist teachers emphasize that eating and drinking here are purely figures of speech for drawing near to Christ and trusting Him. Because the Lord's Supper had not yet been started and taking church communion cannot grant eternal life, they read these words as a call to personal faith rather than a reference to the church ordinance (a sacred practice commanded by Jesus).
differ.disputed: eating his flesh: the Lord's Supper

notes.meaning: Jesus' sacrifice provides the only true nourishment for the human soul. Just as bread and drink strengthen the physical body, relying on his death feeds and sustains our inner life for eternity.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics hold that Jesus' words go beyond symbolism, meaning his flesh and blood are truly present as real food and drink in the sacrament.

notes.meaning: Believing in Jesus brings about a close and lasting union between him and the believer. We live in him by trusting his death, and he lives in us through his Spirit and truth.
The Father is the unending source of life, and the Son lives in complete union with him. In the same way, anyone who draws life from Jesus by faith will live forever because of that shared life.
Jesus brings his teaching back to the comparison with the manna in the wilderness. Earthly bread could only briefly delay death, but Jesus gives everlasting life to anyone who receives him.
Jesus spoke these profound truths openly in the public place of Jewish worship in Capernaum. Speaking publicly in the synagogue gave everyone a chance to hear his message about his coming sacrifice.

Many of the wider group following Jesus found his words offensive and hard to tolerate. They could not accept the idea of feeding on his flesh and blood or recognizing that his kingdom was spiritual rather than worldly.
Without anyone telling him, Jesus knew the secret complaints and stumbling blocks in their hearts. He challenged them to see that the problem was not his words, but their own refusal to believe.

Jesus pointed ahead to his return to heaven, which would prove he truly came from God. His future ascension would also make it clear that he was not talking about people physically eating his body on earth.

Real spiritual life comes only through the Holy Spirit, not through human effort or earthly thinking. Jesus' teachings are spiritual truths that bring eternal life to those who receive them through the Spirit.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics explain that when Jesus said 'the flesh profits nothing,' he was referring to fallen human nature and natural understanding, not calling his own sacrificed flesh useless.

notes.meaning: Jesus pointed out that some in the crowd had never truly trusted him, which is why they missed the life in his words. Because he knows the human heart completely, he knew from the start who lacked true faith and that Judas would eventually betray him.

Jesus reminded them that coming to him in saving faith is a gift from God, not something people can accomplish on their own. Without the Father's drawing and grace, human hearts remain stuck in darkness and unbelief.

differ.view: Coming to Christ happens only through God's effective grace, which overcomes human inability and grants faith to his chosen people.
God offers his enabling grace, but coming to Christ is granted only to those who freely choose to receive it on God's terms.

notes.meaning: After hearing these demanding teachings, many who had followed Jesus walked away and abandoned him for good. His words tested their hearts and revealed that they were only casual followers rather than true believers.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics note that these disciples left because they took Jesus' words about eating his flesh literally, showing that Jesus did not intend his words as mere symbols.

notes.meaning: With the large crowd walking away, Jesus turned to his twelve chosen apostles and asked if they also wanted to abandon him. He asked this not out of fear, but to test and strengthen their personal commitment to him.

Peter spoke up on behalf of the group, declaring that no other teacher could offer what Jesus provides. They knew that leaving him meant turning toward death, because his words alone lead to everlasting life.
Peter confessed their settled assurance that Jesus is the promised Messiah, set apart by God. Their journey with him had turned their initial faith into deep and confident conviction.
Jesus reminded them that he had chosen all twelve to be his close apostles, yet one among them was acting on the side of the enemy. Even within this intimate group of leaders, one would betray him.

differ.view: Methodists believe Jesus truly chose all twelve to be his followers, but Judas showed that a chosen person can fall away through unfaithfulness.
Reformed Christians believe Jesus chose the Twelve only to the office of apostleship, not to eternal salvation, because God's elect can never fall away.

notes.meaning: The writer clarifies that Jesus was talking about Judas Iscariot, who was already harboring betrayal in his heart. Even though Judas shared the special privilege of being an apostle, he would eventually hand Jesus over to his enemies.
